title: Temporary Shortage List: Stage 2 report (accessible)
date_evidence:
Accredited official statistics

# Summary of latest statistics

Published 23 July 2026
key_claim: The MAC assessed 82 mid-skill (RQF 3-5) occupations at Stage 2 of its Temporary Shortage List review. Jobs Plans, the sector workforce strategies that condition access, were received for only 46 of the 82; the remaining 36, more than 40% of the occupations in scope but around 20% of visa usage among the 82, received none. The MAC recommended 28 occupations for the TSL, all of them for 18 months rather than the standard three years, because no occupation submitted a plan strong enough to merit full access. Those 28 occupations account for around 4,000 visas a year across roughly 1.3 million employed. The Committee records that it was lenient on the shortage test against a general loosening of the labour market.
frame_summary: The MAC is arguing that time-limited visa access for mid-skill occupations should be earned by a credible sector plan to reduce reliance on migration, and that on this round's evidence none of those plans has earned more than a probationary term.
verbatim_quote: Under the current framework, we have recommended 28 occupations receive 18-month access to the TSL and none warrant full access through to the next TSL review which we expect to be in three years’ time.
verbatim_list: The Jobs Plan requirement is the largest departure from previous shortage-list processes.
We received Jobs Plans for 46 of the 82 occupations which progressed to Stage 2 of our review.

We did not receive Jobs Plans for 36 of the 82 occupations that were in scope for Stage 2 of our report. Whilst these 36 represent more than 40% of the occupations within Stage 2 of the review, they were generally smaller users of the immigration system, only accounting for around 20% of visa usage amongst the 82 occupations.

We interpret the non-submission of a Jobs Plan as a conscious decision by the relevant government department(s) based on the need for TSL access and/or the likelihood of a given occupation passing the criteria for access.
We did not feel that any occupations provided a strong enough plan to address shortages through utilising the domestic workforce to merit full three-year TSL access.
When making assessments for individual occupations, we were lenient in looking for any signs of shortage relative to the wider trend of reducing shortages across the economy.

A loosening labour market is also reported by institutions such as the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), the Bank of England and corroborated by wider data points on spare capacity in the labour market.

title: Immigration system statistics, year ending June 2026: Summary of latest statistics
key_claim: 235,000 work visas including dependants were granted in the year ending June 2026, 18% fewer than the previous year and 62% below the December 2023 peak. Within that, 120,000 Worker visas were issued, 76% below the same peak, with the fall driven by Health and Care Worker and Skilled Worker grants down 90% and 48% respectively. Work-route extensions were broadly stable at 731,000.
frame_summary: The Home Office is reporting, not arguing, but the release presents the post-2023 restriction package as having produced a sustained and broad-based contraction in work migration rather than a one-off dip.
verbatim_quote: this fall was due to decreases in Health and Care Worker (primarily care workers) and Skilled Worker visas issued, down 90% and 48% respectively over this period
verbatim_list: there were 235,000 work visas granted (including dependants) in the YE (year ending) June 2026, 18% fewer than the previous year and 62% fewer than in the YE (year ending) December 2023, when the number of work visas issued peaked
the number of extensions granted on work routes remained broadly stable in the latest year at 731,000, following increases since 2021
notes: Accredited official statistics. GOV.UK renders abbreviations inline as 'YE (year ending)', so spans containing that token were avoided in favour of clean plain-text spans.

title: Labour market overview, UK: August 2026
date_evidence: Office for National Statistics (ONS), released 18 August 2026, ONS website, statistical bulletin, Labour market overview, UK: August 2026
key_claim: UK vacancies fell to 707,000 in May to July 2026, down 6,000 on the quarter; outside the pandemic period the last comparable level was late 2014. The unemployment rate was 4.9% in April to June 2026, up 0.2 percentage points on the year, and the 16-64 employment rate was 75.1%. ONS vacancy survey feedback attributes some of the weakness to small firms holding back on recruitment because of labour costs and other operating expenses.
frame_summary: ONS is reporting rather than arguing, but the bulletin frames the current vacancy weakness as cost-driven employer restraint in a loosening market rather than as evidence that skills scarcity has been resolved.
verbatim_quote: Outside of the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic period, the last time there were 707,000 or fewer vacancies was in September to November 2014, when there were 703,000 vacancies.
verbatim_list: The UK unemployment rate for people aged 16 years and over was estimated at 4.9% in April to June 2026.
Feedback from our Vacancy Survey suggests that some small firms may not be recruiting because of increases in labour costs and other operating expenses.
notes: Correct edition for a 13 September 2026 scan date: the page states the next release is 15 September 2026. ONS flags Labour Force Survey quality caveats, so the 4.9% unemployment rate is used as directional context rather than as a precise anchor.

title: Skills England annual skills report 2026
date_evidence: meta-govuk:first-published-at: 2026-06-01T08:00:00+01:00 (on-page: "Published 1 June 2026"; HTML version of the annual report added 6 July 2026)
key_claim: Skills England projects Industrial Strategy priority occupations growing 24% to 2035, an extra 1.8 million jobs, against 14% for non-priority occupations. On the survey measure, the share of vacancies constrained by skills shortages fell from 36% in 2022 to 27% in 2024, though shortages remain above pre-pandemic levels with particular problems in construction, education and manufacturing. Skills England states that work is underway across government on Jobs Plans as sector-led workforce plans for the eight Industrial Strategy priority sectors plus construction.
frame_summary: Skills England is arguing that domestic skills supply must be expanded and steered towards Industrial Strategy priority occupations, with sector-led Jobs Plans as the instrument, rather than that persistent shortages justify continued reliance on migration.
verbatim_quote: Building on the Industrial Strategy sector plans, work is underway across government on Jobs Plans. These are sector-led workforce plans that will set out how the 8 industrial strategy priority sectors and construction will tackle workforce shortages and the underlying causes - such as skills gaps, retention, pay, and job quality.
verbatim_list: Priority occupations are projected to grow by 24% to 2035 (1.8 million extra jobs) while non-priority occupations are expected to grow by 14%.
fewer vacancies are constrained by skills shortages, falling from 36% in 2022 to 27% in 2024.
Nevertheless, skills shortages remain stubborn over the long term. They are still above that seen before the COVID-19 pandemic, with particular problems in construction, education and manufacturing.
notes: Single permitted structural anchor for this scan: first published 1 June 2026, 104 days before scan date, therefore in the 3-6 month band. It is the canonical statement of what a Jobs Plan is and of Skills England's role inside the Labour Market Evidence Group that grades them. HTML versions of the annual report and the sectoral skills needs assessments were added on 6 July and 4 August 2026; the earlier first-published date is recorded rather than the later update.

title: Why the UK Must Put Labour Supply At the Heart of its Visa Access Policy
date_evidence: meta-og:image: https://www.cgdev.org/sites/default/files/2026-08/uk-visa.jpeg ; on-page byline "Samuel Huckstep and Helen Dempster / August 10, 2026"
key_claim: CGD assesses the MAC's Stage 2 recommendations and finds them broadly sensible but built on uneven narrative evidence. It notes the 28 recommended occupations account for around 3,800 of the 9,700 annual visas issued in recent years, that Jobs Plans were submitted for just 46 of 82 occupations, and that Skilled Worker visa holders made up an average of 27% of new workforce entrants to the 82 occupations considered. It warns that 18 months is a workable period for improving a plan but a very challenging one for raising trained-worker throughput, because several included occupations have training lengths of 40 months or more.
frame_summary: CGD is arguing that the UK's visa-access process still fails to assess labour supply properly, and that a formal withdrawal-impact test and measured training-throughput benchmarks should replace the current reliance on departmental narrative evidence.
verbatim_quote: Several included occupations have training lengths of 40 months or more, and high apprenticeship attrition rates.
verbatim_list: Those 28 occupations account for around 3,800 of the 9,700 annual visas issued in recent years.
In total, Jobs Plans were submitted for just 46 of the 82 occupations under review.
They ranked #24 on our index: visas account for around 62 percent of observed new entrants, and replacing them would require apprenticeship starts to rise by around 122 percent.
Few Jobs Plans compared projected future demand with likely supply of suitably skilled workers.
notes: CGD writes percentages out as "percent"; verbatim spans preserve the source's wording while the article body uses the house % style. Authors Huckstep and Dempster have published advocacy for wider labour-migration access, so the assessment is interested rather than neutral, though its quantitative index is published separately.

publisher: CIPD (Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development)
title: Labour Market Outlook, Summer 2026
key_claim: Surveying 2,017 employers between 24 June and 24 July 2026, CIPD finds private-sector recruitment intentions at a record low of 57% and total vacancies 10% below pre-pandemic levels, yet 31% of employers still report hard-to-fill vacancies. The share of construction employers anticipating significant problems filling vacancies over the next six months rose from 9% to 23% in a single quarter. CIPD reads the combination as skills mismatch rather than aggregate scarcity, and warns that suppressed entry-level and apprenticeship intake now compounds future hard-to-fill vacancies.
frame_summary: CIPD is arguing that a slack headline labour market is concealing a persistent skills-mismatch problem, and that employers should protect apprenticeship and entry-level intake precisely when hiring is frozen.
verbatim_quote: Our data suggests that despite the low level of vacancies in the economy, three in 10 (31%) employers still have hard-to-fill vacancies.
verbatim_list: The percentage of employers in construction anticipating significant problems in filling vacancies over the next six months has increased considerably from 9% last quarter to 23%, and problems continue to be anticipated in care, social work and other healthcare activities, as well as in human health activities (both at 23%).
Just 57% of employers in the private sector plan to recruit over the next three months, which is the lowest figure since we began collecting this measure in 2016 (outside of the pandemic).
Reduced recruitment, especially of entry-level and younger workers, risks compounding future hard-to-fill vacancies once demand recovers.
notes: Cited at the report PDF rather than the CIPD landing page because the landing page carries stale template metadata (an article:modified_time from 2023) while the PDF colophon and the page's published_time agree on August 2026. Survey data is YouGov-collected, employer-weighted and self-reported; CIPD represents HR practitioners, so treat the employer sentiment figures as directional.

title: CITB publishes Construction Workforce Outlook 2026-2030
key_claim: CITB's Construction Workforce Outlook 2026-2030, modelled with Oxford Economics, finds construction needs an average of 41,200 extra workers a year between 2026 and 2030, equivalent to 1.6% of the 2025 workforce or around 206,000 over five years, with the workforce rising only from 2,606,380 in 2025 to about 2,681,800 in 2030. Output is forecast to contract 0.2% in 2026, so the requirement is mostly replacement demand. CITB attributes the gap to too few entrants, too many experienced leavers and insufficient productivity improvement.
frame_summary: CITB is arguing that construction's workforce gap is replacement-driven and durable rather than cyclical, so training capacity has to be sustained through a weak market rather than tuned to short-horizon policy signals.
verbatim_quote: This will increasingly put a strain on the industry’s capacity to deliver on housing, infrastructure and retrofit commitments.
verbatim_list: An average of 41,200 extra workers will be needed each year between 2026 and 2030. This is equivalent to 1.6% of the 2025 workforce, or around 206,000 additional workers over the five year period.
too many experienced workers are leaving, and productivity improvements have not been sufficient to close the gap
notes: Split-page provenance, stated plainly: the dated news page carries the narrative spans, while the 41,200 figure sits on the linked companion Construction Workforce Outlook tool page at https://www.citb.co.uk/cwo/index.html, which is undated but whose published chart data file is named for June 2026. The verbatim_quote is taken from the dated news page so it is re-fetchable at the cited URL; the 41,200 span is recorded in verbatim_list and attributed in the body to CITB's Outlook rather than to the news page alone. CITB is a levy-funded non-departmental public body with a direct institutional interest in training funding, so the pipeline number is interested-party evidence. The prior Outlook put the annual requirement nearer 47,000, so this is a downward revision.

title: Government confirms incoming construction jobs plan
key_claim: The housing minister confirmed that a construction Jobs Plan is in drafting. The National Federation of Builders argues that because small and medium builders train 8 in 10 construction apprentices they are central to capacity growth, and contrasts the 1980s, when SMEs built around 40% of homes and trained more than 20,000 bricklayers and carpenters, with 2026, when SMEs build 9% of homes and fewer than 20,000 construction apprentices are trained in total.
frame_summary: The trade press and the builders' federation are arguing that a construction Jobs Plan will not raise training capacity unless it is built around the small firms that actually take apprentices.
verbatim_quote: because SMEs train 8 in 10 construction apprentices, they are key to capacity growth
verbatim_list: In the 1980's, SMEs built around 40% of homes and we trained more than 20,000 bricklayers and carpenters. In 2026, SMEs build 9% of homes and in total, fewer than 20.000 construction apprentices get trained.
notes: Specialist trade press reporting a ministerial confirmation and quoting the National Federation of Builders, which is an interested party. The "20.000" decimal point in the second span is a typographical error in the original and is preserved verbatim. Published six days before the scan date and used to establish that the Jobs Plan machinery is still being drafted rather than settled.
